definition: Useful for getting a quick or easy result, even if it is not entirely fair or right.
example: Skipping the safety review was expedient, but it left the bridge project open to costly mistakes.
nuance: Unlike expeditious, which means fast and efficient, expedient suggests choosing convenience, often at some cost to principle.
prompt: A team running late on a science project must decide how to finish it in time.
options: Copying last year's chart was expedient, though the team knew it was not quite honest.
The team hoped to expedient the project by working through lunch and staying late after school.
The expedient plan required months of extra work and helped no one finish on time.
The most expedient student on the team typed ninety words a minute.
reasons: A shortcut that saves time while bending the rules fits the word exactly.
The word is an adjective; this sentence confuses it with the verb expedite.
A slow, unhelpful plan is the opposite of a convenient shortcut.
The word describes a convenient course of action, not a person's raw speed.

practice.prompt: A restaurant owner faces a sudden shortage of fresh basil on a busy night.
options: Swapping in dried basil was an expedient fix, though regular diners noticed the flatter taste.
The owner went on an expedient into the hills to search for wild basil.
Driving four hours to a distant farm for basil was the most expedient choice she could make.
Out of deep respect for her recipes, the owner made the expedient decision to close until fresh basil arrived.
reasons: A quick substitute that solves the problem but costs some quality shows the word's meaning.
This confuses the adjective with expedition, a noun meaning a journey.
A long, costly trip is the reverse of a handy, convenient solution.
Closing to protect standards puts principle first; the word implies favoring convenience instead.
